summary.text: Coastal upwelling is the best-known type of upwelling, where wind blowing along a coast brings deep water up to replace surface water near shore.
When the wind runs parallel to the coastline, Ekman transport carries surface water away from the coast, and deeper, colder, denser water rises in its place.
It supports some of the world's most productive fisheries, mainly along the Canary, Benguela, California and Humboldt currents.

facts.label: Strongest zone
facts.value: Off Luderitz, in the Benguela system

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: Year-round in some regions, seasonal in others

paragraphs.heading: Upwelling at the shore
paragraphs.text: Upwelling is the wind-driven rise of dense, cool deep water, usually rich in nutrients, which replaces the warmer surface water above it. Scientists list at least five kinds, and coastal upwelling is the best known of them. It is also the kind most tied to human life, since some of the richest fisheries on the planet depend on it.

paragraphs.heading: How the wind lifts the water
paragraphs.text: Coastal upwelling happens when the wind blows parallel to the coastline and sets currents moving. The Coriolis effect bends these currents: in the Northern Hemisphere they turn right of the wind, and in the Southern Hemisphere they turn left. The overall result is surface water moving at right angles to the wind, which is called Ekman transport. When that transport carries water away from the shore, deeper, colder and denser water rises to take its place. This usually happens at about 5–10 meters per day, but the wind's strength and reach can change both the rate and how close to the coast the rising occurs.

paragraphs.heading: Why the sea turns rich
paragraphs.text: Deep water holds nutrients such as nitrate, phosphate and silicic acid, left by dead plankton that sank and decayed. At the surface, phytoplankton use these nutrients, along with dissolved CO₂ and sunlight, to make organic compounds by photosynthesis. Upwelling regions therefore have very high primary production, the amount of carbon fixed by phytoplankton, and they provide about 50% of the ocean's productivity worldwide. That plenty spreads upward, because phytoplankton form the base of the ocean food chain.

paragraphs.heading: Year-round and seasonal
paragraphs.text: In some places coastal upwelling goes on all year; these are called major coastal upwelling systems. In others it happens only in certain months, and these are seasonal coastal upwelling systems. Many of these systems have fairly high carbon productivity and are classed as Large Marine Ecosystems. Five major coastal currents are linked to upwelling: the Canary Current near Northwest Africa, the Benguela Current near southern Africa, the California Current along California and Oregon, the Humboldt Current along Peru and Chile, and the Somali Current near Somalia and Oman. Each of them supports major fisheries.

paragraphs.heading: The four eastern boundary currents
paragraphs.text: Most coastal upwelling happens in four eastern boundary currents: the Canary, Benguela, California and Humboldt currents. The Benguela, on the eastern edge of the South Atlantic gyre, has a northern and a southern part, split by permanent upwelling off Luderitz, the strongest upwelling zone on Earth. The California Current also splits, at Point Conception, with weak upwelling to the south and strong upwelling to the north. The Canary Current is divided by the Canary Islands, and the Humboldt Current runs along South America from Peru to Chile, reaching as far as 1,000 kilometers out to sea.
